briefing.opening: Hello everyone. We will now begin the climate briefing for October 6, 2026.

sections.title: 🌍 Deepening International Climate Litigation and Liability Discussions
sections.content: The U.S. Supreme Court has commenced its new term with major climate change-related lawsuits, hearing arguments on who should bear the costs of climate change and the liability of energy companies [14, 132, 138, 141-173]. Climate change lawsuits filed by local governments against oil and gas companies have emerged as a key issue before the Supreme Court [172, 180], further strengthening arguments that the oil industry should pay for the costs of climate change [139]. These legal developments reflect the international community's efforts to clarify the issue of responsibility between perpetrators and victims of climate change [4].

sections.title: ⚠️ Domestic and International Climate Change Impacts and Crisis Warnings
sections.content: Extreme weather phenomena due to climate change are posing serious threats both domestically and internationally. In Japan, 'extreme weather inflation' occurred, with vegetable prices rising 2.4 times due to 37 consecutive days of rain [19]. Domestically, the risk of forest fires has increased due to climate change, leading Donghae City to deploy response personnel, and Gangwon's fishing industry faces the crisis of village disappearance [11, 13]. Furthermore, international relief and development NGO Plan warned that the climate crisis increases the risk of girls dropping out of school and child marriage [15]. Reports also indicate that climate change is impacting milk and egg quality and making ecological threats like killer mosquitoes and rabid bats a reality [135, 181]. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese also emphasized the urgency of the climate crisis, warning that his country would face a dangerous summer including floods, cyclones, and extreme heat [184].

sections.title: 🌱 South Korea Accelerates Carbon Neutrality Implementation
sections.content: Various local governments and industries across South Korea are accelerating efforts to achieve carbon neutrality. Uijeongbu City is strengthening its policies by establishing a foundation for carbon neutrality implementation and reorganizing environment-related departments [16, 46, 47]. Suwon Special City is encouraging citizen participation by hosting a Carbon Neutrality Festival, and Geoje City is operating 'visiting carbon neutrality promotional booths' [31, 33, 42]. Despite the construction downturn, the ready-mixed concrete industry is pursuing management innovation by exploring carbon neutrality and AI responses [24, 29, 32, 34, 36, 40, 41]. Furthermore, the 'Gyeonggi Climate Satellite No. 2' for greenhouse gas observation was successfully launched, expected to contribute to achieving carbon neutrality goals [20].

sections.title: 🇰🇷 Renewable Energy Transition Goals and Challenges
sections.content: Minister of Climate Kim Sung-hwan announced the goal of achieving 100 GW of renewable energy by 2030, expressing a commitment to become a leading decarbonization nation [51, 65, 67, 76, 81, 85, 86, 88, 89, 114, 115, 116, 117, 120, 123, 124]. To this end, power grid system redesign and adjustments to solar power regulations and grid connections are planned [50, 63, 64]. The Korea Energy Agency is also expanding international cooperation by supporting domestic renewable energy companies' entry into the Vietnamese market [55, 57, 58, 59, 60, 62, 68, 78, 79, 101]. However, challenges remain in expanding the power grid and ensuring stable grid connection, such as increased renewable energy output curtailment and 3.5 GW of renewable energy facilities awaiting grid connection in the Jeonnam-Gwangju region [94, 107, 112], necessitating the development of feasible plans [72].

briefing.closing: Today's briefing highlighted the complex impacts of climate change, the legal and policy responses to it, and the challenges of renewable energy transition. International cooperation and domestic efforts to overcome the climate crisis are more urgent than ever. This concludes today's climate briefing.
